results.name: early_session_yes_excess
results.description: Yes rate on trials with trial_index < 90 minus yes rate on later trials; observed > null means people say yes more early in the session than the (time-invariant) model reproduces.

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate when the target is itself one of the shown examples; observed < null means the model over-predicts near-certain "yes" for already-seen numbers (people lapse/deny more).

results.name: shared_last_digit_match_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples all ending in the same digit, yes rate for unseen targets that also end in that digit; observed < null means the model over-commits to "ends in d" rules (people endorse them less), observed > null under-commits.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_match_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples all ending in the same digit, yes rate for unseen targets that also end in that digit; observed < null means the model over-commits to "ends in d" rules (people endorse them less), observed > null under-commits.
def test_statistic(df):
    a = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    valid = ~np.isnan(a)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    d = np.where(valid, np.mod(a, 10), np.nan)
    d0 = d[:, 0]
    same = (np.where(valid, d == d0[:, None], True)).all(axis=1)
    inset = (a == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & same & ~inset & (np.mod(t, 10) == d0)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: proximity_gradient_outside_range
results.description: For targets outside the examples' range, yes rate at distance 1-5 from the nearest example minus yes rate at distance 11-30; observed > null means people show a steeper similarity/proximity gradient when extrapolating than the model's interval hypotheses produce.
results.code:
# name: proximity_gradient_outside_range
# description: For targets outside the examples' range, yes rate at distance 1-5 from the nearest example minus yes rate at distance 11-30; observed > null means people show a steeper similarity/proximity gradient when extrapolating than the model's interval hypotheses produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    a = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mind = np.nanmin(np.abs(a - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    out = (t < np.nanmin(a, axis=1)) | (t > np.nanmax(a, axis=1))
    near = out & (mind >= 1) & (mind <= 5)
    far = out & (mind >= 11) & (mind <= 30)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity (target not in set), yes rate for targets of that parity minus targets of the other parity; observed < null means the model over-weights the odd/even rules relative to people, observed > null under-weights them.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity (target not in set), yes rate for targets of that parity minus targets of the other parity; observed < null means the model over-weights the odd/even rules relative to people, observed > null under-weights them.
def test_statistic(df):
    a = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    valid = ~np.isnan(a)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(a, 2), np.nan)
    allodd = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1) == n
    alleven = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1) == n
    inset = (a == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    elig = (n >= 2) & (allodd | alleven) & ~inset
    setpar = np.where(allodd, 1, 0)
    match = elig & (np.mod(t, 2) == setpar)
    mis = elig & (np.mod(t, 2) != setpar)
    if match.sum() == 0 or mis.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[mis].mean())

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets outside the examples' range and more than 20 from every example; observed > null means the model under-produces broad/diffuse "yes" generalisation to remote numbers.
results.code:
# name: far_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets outside the examples' range and more than 20 from every example; observed > null means the model under-produces broad/diffuse "yes" generalisation to remote numbers.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    a = sets.values
    mind = np.nanmin(np.abs(a - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(a, axis=1), np.nanmax(a, axis=1)
    m = (mind > 20) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose set has exactly one example (target not equal to it); observed < null means the model generalises too broadly from one example, observed > null too narrowly.

results.name: consecutive_response_perseveration
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials (trial_index increments by 1) with a different number_set; observed > null means people perseverate on their previous answer beyond what the stimulus-driven model produces.
results.code:
# name: consecutive_response_perseveration
# description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials (trial_index increments by 1) with a different number_set; observed > null means people perseverate on their previous answer beyond what the stimulus-driven model produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    consec = (ti[1:] == ti[:-1] + 1) & (s[1:] != s[:-1])
    prev, cur = r[:-1][consec], r[1:][consec]
    if (prev == 1).sum() == 0 or (prev == 0).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(cur[prev == 1].mean() - cur[prev == 0].mean())
